lessons.title: Ionic and covalent bonding
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding; structure and properties (to be checked against the official syllabus)

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why atoms form bonds (to obtain a full outer shell).
Describe ionic bonding as electron transfer and write the formulae of ions.
Describe covalent bonding as sharing of electrons and draw dot-and-cross diagrams in words.
Predict the type of bonding from the elements involved.
reviewNotes: Dot-and-cross diagrams are described in words and symbols; hand-drawn diagrams are expected in class.

blocks.title: Ionic bonding
blocks.md: A **metal** atom **loses** outer electrons to form a positive ion (cation); a **non-metal** atom **gains** electrons to form a negative ion (anion). The oppositely charged ions attract strongly (ionic bond) and form a giant lattice. Example: Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron → Na⁺ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Formula **NaCl**. Magnesium oxide: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, formula **MgO**.

blocks.title: Covalent bonding
blocks.md: Two **non-metal** atoms **share** pairs of electrons so that each gets a full outer shell. A shared pair is one **covalent bond**. Examples: H₂ (1 bond), Cl₂ (1), O₂ (**double** bond, 2 pairs), N₂ (**triple** bond, 3 pairs), H₂O (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs on O), NH₃ (3 bonds), CH₄ (4 bonds), CO₂ (2 double bonds). The result is a **molecule**.

blocks.title: Which type of bond?
blocks.md:
- Metal + non-metal → **ionic**.
- Non-metal + non-metal → **covalent**.
- Metal + metal (alloys, or one metal) → **metallic**: positive ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.

The charge of a metal ion in Groups I, II, III is +1, +2, +3; non-metal ions in Groups VI, VII are 2− and 1−.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- In ionic bonding electrons are **transferred**; in covalent bonding they are **shared**.
- Count only the **outer-shell** electrons in diagrams.
- Ionic compounds are not made of molecules: NaCl is a lattice, not 'a NaCl molecule'.

blocks.caption: Formation of sodium chloride: sodium transfers one electron to chlorine.
blocks.alt: Two large circles for sodium and chlorine atoms with a red arrow labelled 1 electron from sodium to chlorine, and the resulting ions Na+ and Cl- below.

blocks.title: Example 1 — magnesium oxide
blocks.statement: Explain the formation of magnesium oxide from magnesium (2,8,2) and oxygen (2,6).
steps: Magnesium loses its 2 outer electrons → Mg²⁺ (2,8). Oxygen gains 2 electrons → O²⁻ (2,8).
The ions have equal and opposite charges (2+ and 2−), so they combine 1 : 1: formula MgO.

blocks.title: Example 2 — water
blocks.statement: Describe the bonding in a molecule of water, H₂O.
steps: Oxygen (2,6) needs 2 more electrons; each hydrogen (1) needs 1.
Oxygen shares one pair with each of two H atoms: 2 covalent bonds; two lone pairs stay on O. Each atom has a full outer shell.

lessons.title: Structure and properties of substances
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding; structure and properties (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe giant ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent and metallic structures.
Relate melting points and electrical conductivity to structure.
Explain the properties of diamond and graphite.
Predict properties of a substance from its structure.
reviewNotes: Melting points are described qualitatively (high/low); no specific numbers apart from NaCl being 'about 800 °C'.
Silicon(IV) oxide is mentioned as a giant covalent substance (sand).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Four types of structure
blocks.md:
- **Giant ionic** (NaCl, MgO): high melting point, brittle, conducts **only when molten or dissolved** (ions free to move), often soluble in water.
- **Simple molecular** (H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, I₂): **low** melting and boiling points (weak forces **between** molecules), do **not** conduct.
- **Giant covalent** (diamond, graphite, silicon(IV) oxide): very high melting points, insoluble.
- **Metallic**: high melting point, conduct electricity and heat, malleable and ductile.

blocks.title: Diamond and graphite
blocks.md: Both are pure carbon (allotropes). **Diamond**: each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D network, **very hard**, does **not conduct**; used in cutting tools. **Graphite**: layers of carbon atoms, each bonded to 3 others; the layers slide easily (soft, a **lubricant**, used in pencils) and each atom has a free (delocalised) electron so graphite **conducts electricity** (electrodes).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- When a molecular substance melts, only the weak forces **between molecules** are overcome, not the covalent bonds inside the molecules.
- Ionic solids do not conduct electricity (ions fixed); molten or dissolved ones do.
- Metals conduct because of delocalised electrons, not ions.

blocks.caption: A section of the sodium chloride lattice: positive and negative ions alternate in all directions.
blocks.alt: A square grid of alternating blue plus and red minus circles representing sodium and chloride ions.

blocks.title: Example 1 — which is which?
blocks.statement: Substance A: melts at 800 °C, conducts when molten but not as a solid. Substance B: melts at −7 °C and does not conduct. Identify the structure of each.
steps: A: high melting point and conducts only when molten (ions free to move): giant ionic.
B: very low melting point and no conduction: simple molecular.
blocks.answer: A giant ionic; B simple molecular

blocks.title: Example 2 — graphite and diamond
blocks.statement: Explain why graphite is used as a lubricant and as an electrode, while diamond is used for cutting.
steps: Graphite has layers held by weak forces, so they slide over each other (lubricant); free electrons carry charge (electrode).
In diamond every carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid network, so it is extremely hard and cuts glass and rock.
blocks.answer: Layers slide + free electrons; rigid network
